18.text:
MerkleForge is a framework for authenticated data structures, available as Rust crates and
TypeScript packages. You put data in, get a 32-byte root out, and hand out small proofs that
anyone holding the root can check, without downloading the rest of the data.
18.title: Why MerkleForge

19.text:
Data verification is one of the major bottlenecks in modern blockchain networks. As systems
process millions of transactions, checking the integrity of state data gets slow and
resource-intensive. Every state lookup, transaction batch, and light-client proof depends on the
speed and correctness of the underlying data structure. The Rust ecosystem has strong cryptographic building blocks, but Merkle tree support is spread
across variant-specific crates. Libraries like rs-merkle focus on binary trees, while
Ethereum-specific tries are maintained separately. Teams end up stitching together tools with
different APIs, documentation depth, test coverage, and benchmark methodology. JavaScript and TypeScript have the same gap. Libraries like merkletreejs and
@openzeppelin/merkle-tree focus on binary trees, while Ethereum-compatible tries are maintained
separately. Teams end up stitching together tools with different APIs, proof formats, and test
coverage, and proofs made in one language rarely verify in another.
19.title: The problem

20.text:
MerkleForge unifies the three Merkle tree variants used across production systems behind one
API: VariantTypical useBinaryMerkleTree<H>Transaction batching, Bitcoin-style SPV, logs, file chunksSparseMerkleTree<H>Account state, key-value maps, Layer-2 rollupsMerklePatriciaTrie<H>Ethereum state roots, receipts, storage witnesses All three are generic over a HashFunction, implement the shared
MerkleTree<H> trait, and produce proofs that verify statelessly. VariantTypical useBinaryMerkleTreeTransaction batching, airdrops and allowlists, logs, file chunksSparseMerkleTreeAccount state, key-value maps, Layer-2 rollupsMerklePatriciaTrieEthereum state roots, receipts, storage witnesses All three take a HashFunction object at construction, implement
the shared MerkleTree interface, and produce proofs that verify statelessly.
20.title: The solution

21.text:
Unified API. BinaryMerkleTree<H>, SparseMerkleTree<H>, and MerklePatriciaTrie<H> all
implement MerkleTree<H>, so generic code works with any of them.Pluggable hash functions. Swap SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3 by changing one type
parameter. Generics are monomorphised at compile time, so there is no runtime dispatch.Stateless verification. A light client verifies a leaf with the trusted root, the proof, and
the leaf bytes. See Proofs & stateless verification.Domain separation built in. Leaves hash as H(0x00 ‖ data) and internal nodes as
H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right), which blocks second-preimage attacks. See the
mental model.Reproducible benchmarks. A dedicated Criterion suite compares hashes, tree variants, and
other Rust Merkle libraries. See Benchmarks.Tested. Unit, integration, property-based (Proptest), and Ethereum test-vector tests.#![forbid(unsafe_code)] in every published crate. Unified API. BinaryMerkleTree, SparseMerkleTree, and MerklePatriciaTrie all implement
the MerkleTree interface, so generic code works with any of them.Pluggable hash functions. Swap SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3 by passing a different
HashFunction object, for example BinaryMerkleTree.fromLeaves(Keccak256, leaves). The hash is
a value, not a type parameter. @merkleforge/hash-wasm adds WebAssembly Keccak-256 and SHA-256
with identical output.Byte-identical with Rust. Roots, proofs, and proof encodings (bincode and JSON) match the Rust
crates byte for byte, so a Rust server can prove and a browser can verify, or the other way round.Stateless verification. A light client verifies a leaf with the trusted root, the proof, and
the leaf bytes. See Proofs & stateless verification.Domain separation built in. Leaves hash as H(0x00 ‖ data) and internal nodes as
H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right), which blocks second-preimage attacks. See the
mental model.Runs anywhere. ESM only, on Node.js 22+, browsers, Deno, and Bun. The only runtime dependency
is @noble/hashes.Ethereum and on-chain. eth_getProof verification, an OpenZeppelin-compatible
StandardMerkleTree, and Solidity verifiers for Keccak-256 proofs.Tested. Unit, property-based (fast-check), cross-implementation vectors generated from the
Rust crates, and Ethereum test-vector tests.

Think of a Merkle root as a fingerprint for many values. Change any value and the fingerprint
changes. A proof is the short path that lets another machine check one value against that

37.title: The four pieces

38.text:
The prover (a server, indexer, or full node) holds the full tree. It publishes the root and
answers proof requests.The verifier (a light client, browser, contract, or embedded device) holds only a trusted
root, for example from a block header or a signed checkpoint. A proof is only as good as the root you check it against. Get the root from a source you trust.
38.title: Who holds what

39.text:
MerkleForge hashes leaves and internal nodes in different domains: HashPre-imageLeafH(0x00 ‖ data)Internal nodeH(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right) Without the prefixes, an internal node's pre-image (left ‖ right, 64 bytes) is also a valid leaf
value. An attacker could then present an internal node as if it were a leaf and forge a "proof"
for data that was never inserted. This is a second-preimage attack. With distinct prefixes, a
leaf hash can never equal an internal node hash for a different structure. The Sha256 and Keccak256 adapters use the byte prefixes above. Blake3 gets the same
separation from BLAKE3's derive_key mode with two context strings. See
Hash functions for the exact constructions.
39.title: Domain separation: 0x00 and 0x01

40.title: Verifying by hand

41.text:
BinaryMerkleTree pads the leaf layer to the next power of two with H::empty()hasher.empty(),
the hash of an empty leaf. Five leaves become eight slots.SparseMerkleTree has 2²⁵⁶ slots and precomputes the root of an empty subtree at every level,
so empty regions cost nothing to store.MerklePatriciaTrie follows Ethereum's node layout and has no padding. Because empty slots hash to H::empty()hasher.empty(), empty leaf data is rejected with
MerkleError::EmptyLeafDataa MerkleError with code 'EmptyLeafData'; otherwise an inserted empty value would be indistinguishable from
padding.
41.title: Padding and empty slots

42.text:
MerkleProof::leaf_countMerkleProof.leafCount tells the verifier how deep the path should be. The root does not
commit to it, so any count with the same padded size verifies. If the exact number of leaves matters
to you, get it from a trusted source and compare.

# or

94.text:
Lower elapsed time: construction finished sooner.Lower power/energy-pkg/ Joules: the CPU package used less energy.Fewer cycles for the same workload: less CPU work.Cache misses explain why runs with similar hash speed differ in time or energy. Energy measurements are hardware-specific. Report the machine, kernel, CPU governor, Rust version,
and command line with every table. BLAKE3's lower cycles per byte usually means less energy per
proof, which is why the suite measures all three algorithms. The full guide lives in

94.title: Interpreting results

95.text:
The Rust crates and the TypeScript packages are benchmarked separately, each with its own harness.
Lower latency is better; higher throughput is better. Results are hardware-specific: compare
trends across machines, not absolute values. MerkleForge uses Criterion benchmarks in the unpublished
merkle-bench crate to compare hash adapters, tree variants, proof generation, proof
verification, and other Rust Merkle libraries. Criterion reports mean, median, and standard
deviation to filter out noise. For the latest CI numbers with links to every Criterion report, see
the live benchmark explorer. The tables below are copied from BENCHMARKS.md
(run date 2026-08-17). That run predates the v0.5.0 sparse-tree and Patricia-trie

114.text:
Fallible MerkleForge operations report a MerkleError. Verification functions return a boolean
instead: a bad proof is an expected outcome, not an error. Every fallible MerkleForge API returns Result<T, MerkleError>. MerkleError lives in merkle_core::error (and the prelude). It implements Debug, Clone,
PartialEq, Eq, Display, and, with the default std feature, std::error::Error, so it works
with ?, Box<dyn Error>, anyhow, and thiserror. Every fallible MerkleForge API throws a MerkleError. It is exported from @merkleforge/core and
extends the built-in Error, so try/catch, instanceof Error, and error reporting tools work
as usual. Each error carries a detail object whose code names the case (also available as
error.code), plus that case's fields. isMerkleError(error, code?) is a type guard that narrows
detail to the given code.

156.text:
Proofs have two wire formats shared by both languages: a compact binary encoding
(bincode 2, standard config) and a JSON shape (what
serde_json produces). A proof encoded in Rust decodes in TypeScript, and the other way round. Proofs and trees implement serde's Serialize and Deserialize. On top of that, merkle-core
provides the Serializable trait with compact binary helpers backed by bincode. Proofs are plain objects and trees are classes, so there is no serde or trait to derive.
Instead, each proof type has a pair of explicit codecs for each format, all of which produce the
same bytes or JSON as the Rust crates: ProofBinary (bincode)Rust-compatible JSONMerkleProof (@merkleforge/core)encodeMerkleProof / decodeMerkleProofmerkleProofToSerdeJSON / merkleProofFromSerdeJSONSparseMerkleProofencodeSparseProof / decodeSparseProofsparseProofToSerdeJSON / sparseProofFromSerdeJSONMptProofencodeMptProof / decodeMptProofmptProofToSerdeJSON / mptProofFromSerdeJSONBinaryMultiProofencodeBinaryMultiProof / decodeBinaryMultiProofmultiProofToSerdeJSON / multiProofFromSerdeJSON The sparse, Patricia, and multiproof codecs are exported from @merkleforge/variants. take an optional digestSize (default 32) where the proof holds fixed-size digests.

161.text:
TreeMetadata implements Serialize and Deserialize, but its string fields are
&'static str, so it can't be deserialized from an owned buffer and is not Serializable.
Serialize it for logs and dashboards, for example with serde_json::to_string(&tree.metadata()). TreeMetadata is a plain object, so JSON.stringify(tree.metadata()) works and JSON.parse
reads it back. Its keys are camelCase (leafCount, nodeCount, …), not the snake_case keys Rust
writes. See Metadata.
